title: Why Do Leaders Tolerate Poor Performers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short, direct article catalogs the rationalizations leaders use to avoid confronting poor performers -- misplaced loyalty, conflict avoidance, sunk-cost thinking, senior sponsorship, and personal guilt -- and argues that each of these rationalizations, however understandable, destroys the leader's credibility and undermines team culture. The piece draws on research showing that HR executives trust fewer than 40% of leaders to hold poor performers accountable, and that tolerating poor performance is the second most common reason boards fire CEOs. The article's core claim is that high performers on the team watch how leaders treat low performers and draw conclusions about whether excellence is rewarded or undermined; when leaders tolerate incompetence, the best people leave and the standards collapse for everyone who remains. The author concludes that good leaders never excuse weak performance -- they tackle it head-on, understanding that loyalty to a colleague must never supersede the leader's accountability to the team and the mission.
points: * Covering for a poor performer signals to high performers that excellence is not actually valued, which causes the best people to leave in disgust -- the leader's attempt to avoid conflict ends by losing exactly the people the team most needs to keep. * Research found that HR executives trust fewer than 40% of leaders to hold poor performers accountable; and the second most common reason boards fire CEOs is tolerating poor performance -- not far behind weak long-term company performance. * Many leaders wait for a turnaround that 'usually never arrives,' holding onto an image of the team member at their best rather than engaging the reality of current performance; this is a form of hope that functions as neglect. * Leaders who give candid feedback to some people while letting others spin out of control look like they are playing favorites, which undermines the entire culture of accountability -- you cannot hold the team to standards selectively. * The rationalizations for avoiding poor-performer conversations are legion and some are genuinely sympathetic (rough patch, institutional knowledge, ongoing project); the article's point is that they are still rationalizations, and good leaders recognize them as such and act anyway.
quotes: Tolerating poor performers is a common failure for far too many leaders. Inexplicably, leaders and managers who know better cover for weak performers and offer a wide variety of rationalizations for doing so.

Many leaders want to avoid conflict and dislike difficult conversations. They find that giving candid feedback and working through low performance can be emotionally draining, so problems get postponed.
Other leaders remember when the team member was strong and showed potential, and they are not ready to give up on that image. They keep waiting for a turnaround that usually never arrives.

A recent study of human resources executives found they trust less than 40 percent of leaders and managers to hold poor performers accountable. A separate study found the second most common reason boards fire a CEO is for tolerating poor performance -- not far behind weak long-term company performance.
High performers often leave the team in disgust, believing excellence is undermined when leaders tolerate incompetence.
When leaders refuse to address poor performance, bystanders and stakeholders lose confidence and trust in them.
Rationalizations for avoiding the need to address the poor performer are legion. But good leaders never excuse weak performance. They tackle it head-on.
